# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of significant epicardial coronary stenosis [1]. First described in detail by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the condition has since been recognized as a distinct clinical and angiographic disorder rather than a mere incidental finding [2]. CSFP is frequently encountered during diagnostic coronary angiography, particularly in patients presenting with chest pain and otherwise unobstructed coronary arteries [3]. Despite decades of investigation, the pathophysiology remains incompletely understood, and management strategies are largely empirical [4].

## Definition and Quantification

The introduction of the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count by Gibson et al. provided an objective, reproducible method to quantify coronary flow [5]. CSFP is conventionally diagnosed when the corrected TIMI frame count exceeds two standard deviations above the normal mean for a given vessel [6]. This standardization has facilitated comparison across studies and improved diagnostic consistency [7]. The phenomenon most commonly affects the left anterior descending artery, although multivessel involvement is well documented [8].

## Epidemiology

CSFP is reported in approximately 1–7% of patients undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia [3,9]. It demonstrates a male predominance and tends to affect younger patients, frequently with a history of smoking [9,10]. Many affected individuals have recurrent presentations to emergency departments, contributing to considerable healthcare utilization [10].

## Pathophysiology

The mechanisms underlying CSFP remain a subject of active research, with several overlapping hypotheses proposed. Microvascular dysfunction is widely regarded as a central contributor, supported by histopathological findings of myointimal hyperplasia, endothelial degeneration, and capillary abnormalities on endomyocardial biopsy [11]. Endothelial dysfunction, evidenced by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilation, has been consistently demonstrated [12,13]. Elevated markers of systemic inflammation, including high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, suggest a role for subclinical inflammation [14].

Diffuse atherosclerosis below the threshold of angiographic detection, identified through intravascular ultrasound, has been observed in many patients, indicating that CSFP may represent an early atherosclerotic stage [15]. Abnormal platelet function and a prothrombotic milieu have also been described [16]. Oxidative stress, with increased markers such as malondialdehyde and reduced antioxidant capacity, may further impair microvascular function [17]. Additionally, alterations in cardiac autonomic regulation, reflected by reduced heart rate variability, have been reported [18].

## Clinical Presentation and Associations

The dominant clinical manifestation is recurrent angina, often occurring at rest, and a substantial proportion of patients experience acute coronary syndromes [19]. CSFP has been associated with malignant ventricular arrhythmias and, rarely, sudden cardiac death [20]. Metabolic associations are notable, with links to insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and obesity reported in several cohorts [21,22]. Increased epicardial adipose tissue and elevated serum uric acid have likewise been associated with the phenomenon [23]. Electrocardiographic abnormalities, including prolonged QT dispersion and fragmented QRS complexes, suggest underlying repolarization heterogeneity [24].

## Diagnosis and Imaging

Coronary angiography with TIMI frame count assessment remains the cornerstone of diagnosis [5,6]. Advanced imaging modalities, including myocardial perfusion scintigraphy and cardiac magnetic resonance, can reveal perfusion abnormalities consistent with microvascular involvement [25]. Coronary flow reserve measurement, by Doppler or thermodilution techniques, provides functional confirmation of impaired microvascular function [26].

## Management

There is no universally accepted treatment for CSFP, and therapy is directed at symptom relief and addressing presumed mechanisms [4]. Dipyridamole and nicorandil, agents that enhance microvascular flow, have shown benefit in small studies [27]. Calcium channel blockers, particularly mibefradil and diltiazem, have improved TIMI frame counts and angina frequency [28]. Statins, through their pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilizing effects, may improve coronary flow and symptoms [29]. Lifestyle modification, including smoking cessation and management of metabolic risk factors, is strongly recommended [22].

## Prognosis

Although historically considered benign, accumulating evidence indicates that CSFP carries a non-trivial burden of recurrent angina, repeated hospitalizations, and impaired quality of life [10]. While major adverse cardiovascular events are relatively uncommon, the association with arrhythmias warrants careful clinical follow-up [20,30].

## Conclusion

CSFP is a distinct and clinically relevant angiographic entity with a multifactorial pathophysiology encompassing microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, inflammation, and early atherosclerosis [11,15]. Standardized diagnosis using the TIMI frame count has advanced research, yet substantial gaps remain in understanding its natural history and optimal management [30]. Future large-scale prospective studies are needed to clarify therapeutic strategies and prognostic implications.
